question_text:
Steady-state creep rate data are given in the following table for some alloy taken at $200^{\circ} \mathrm{C}(473 \mathrm{~K})$ :

| $\dot{\varepsilon}{s}\left(\mathrm{~h}^{-1}\right)$ | $\sigma[\mathrm{MPa}(p s i)]$ |
| :-- | :-- |
| $2.5 \times 10^{-3}$ | $55(8000)$ |
| $2.4 \times 10^{-2}$ | $69(10,000)$ |

If it is known that the activation energy for creep is $140,000 \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{mol}$, compute the steady-state creep rate at a temperature of $250^{\circ} \mathrm{C}(523 \mathrm{~K})$ and a stress level of $48 \mathrm{MPa}(7000 \mathrm{psi})$.The unit of the answer is h^-1.
response:
## Solution

The steady-state creep rate follows the power-law (Norton) relation:

$$\dot{\varepsilon}_s = K\,\sigma^{\,n}\,e^{-Q/(RT)}$$

**Step 1 — Stress exponent $n$.** Both data points are at $T_1 = 473\ \text{K}$, so the exponential term cancels in the ratio:

$$\frac{\dot{\varepsilon}_{s2}}{\dot{\varepsilon}_{s1}}=\left(\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\right)^{n}
\;\Rightarrow\;
\frac{2.4\times10^{-2}}{2.5\times10^{-3}}=\left(\frac{69}{55}\right)^{n}
\;\Rightarrow\;
n=\frac{\ln(9.6)}{\ln(1.2545)}\approx 9.97\approx 10$$

**Step 2 — Constant $K$.** Using point 1 with $Q=140{,}000\ \text{J/mol}$ and $R=8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$:

$$K=\frac{\dot{\varepsilon}_{s1}}{\sigma_1^{\,n}\,e^{-Q/(RT_1)}}\approx 3.23\times10^{-5}$$

**Step 3 — Creep rate at $T_2=523\ \text{K}$, $\sigma=48\ \text{MPa}$:**

$$\dot{\varepsilon}_s = K\,(48)^{n}\,e^{-140000/(8.314\cdot523)}\approx 1.93\times10^{-2}\ \text{h}^{-1}$$

The temperature increase (473 → 523 K) raises the rate by a factor of ~34, while the lower stress (55 → 48 MPa) reduces it by a factor of ~0.27, giving a net increase of roughly an order of magnitude.

$$\boxed{1.93\times10^{-2}}$$
